screens.title: Core TCP/IP Concepts: IP, Subnet Mask, Gateway, DNS
screens.narratorSegment: Start with definitions that shape every network decision you make. An IP address is a unique numeric label that identifies a device on an IP network; think of it as a mailing address for packets. The subnet mask is a 32-bit value that partitions that address into the network and host portions — it tells your system which addresses are local and which are remote. The default gateway is the router that forwards traffic destined for other networks; if your host has no route for an address, it sends packets to the gateway. DNS translates human-friendly names into IP addresses so you can reach services by name rather than number. A simple example: your server might have address 192.168.1.100/24, mask /24 means hosts in 192.168.1. x are local, gateway 192.168.1.1 is used for outside traffic, and DNS servers like 8.8.8.8 resolve domain names. A common misconception is thinking DNS or gateway alone will fix all connectivity. If the subnet mask is wrong, a host may incorrectly consider a peer to be local or remote, causing traffic to be misrouted even though the gateway and DNS are correct. Always verify the mask, gateway, and DNS together when diagnosing connectivity issues. Reflect: if you can ping an IP but not a name, which layer is likely at fault?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Core TCP/IP Concepts
Definition: IP Address
A unique label for a device. Example: 192.168.1.100/24 shows host plus mask indicating the local network is 192.168.1.0/24.
Definition: Subnet Mask
Divides the IP into network and host parts. Mistakes here often cause devices to be unreachable even though gateway and DNS are correct.
Definition: Default Gateway
Router that forwards traffic destined for other networks. If ping to external IPs fails but the gateway is reachable, routing beyond the gateway may be blocked.
Definition: DNS
Translates domain names to IP addresses. If you can reach external IPs but not names, DNS is the likely cause.
Concrete example
Given: IP 192.168.1.100/24, gateway 192.168.1.1, DNS 8.8.8.8. You can ping 192.168.1.1 but not google.com. This indicates DNS is failing while local routing is correct. Use dig or nslookup to confirm.
Common mistake
Setting the wrong subnet mask can make hosts appear on different networks, causing asymmetric routing; verify the mask before changing gateway or DNS.
Key Takeaway

Address + mask + gateway + DNS form the minimal set required for basic connectivity; errors in any one can break communication.

screens.title: Inspecting Interfaces with the ip Command
screens.narratorSegment: The ip command is the modern, supported utility for viewing and manipulating Linux networking. To begin, run ip addr show to list interfaces, their IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and link states. You will typically see lo for loopback and a named Ethernet device such as eth0 or enp0s3. Use ip route show to inspect the system routing table; look for a default route that points to your gateway. A practical example: when you suspect a missing address, ip addr show reveals whether the interface is UP and which addresses are configured. If there's no default route, ip route show will indicate that and explain why external traffic fails. For quick temporary testing, the ip command can add an address: use sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3 followed by sudo ip link set enp0s3 up to bring the interface online. Remember these changes are ephemeral and useful for testing before committing persistent files. A common error is reading an interface name as permanent — interface names can differ by kernel and distribution, so always confirm the current name before scripting. After you run these commands, verify with ip addr show and ip route show to confirm your test changes took effect.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Inspect with ip
Read interface state
ip addr show
ip route show
These commands list addresses, link state, and the routing table for diagnosis.
Temporary configuration example
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3
sudo ip link set enp0s3 up
Use these to test connectivity; they will be lost after a reboot.
Annotated output guide
  • Interface name and state (e.g., UP) — shows link readiness.
  • inet lines — list IPv4 addresses and prefix length.
  • ether line — MAC address used for local switching.
  • Default route — destination 0.0.0.0/0 or word default pointing to gateway.
Pitfall
Don’t assume interface names are identical between systems. Confirm the current name before applying scripted changes.
Pro Tip

Use ip commands for quick, reversible testing. Once verified, move changes into persistent configuration files or connection settings.

screens.title: Temporary vs Persistent Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: A crucial operational distinction is temporary versus persistent network changes. Temporary changes made with the ip command are applied only to the running kernel state; they are ideal for experiments, immediate troubleshooting, or short-lived testing because they are safe to revert and do not modify system configuration files. Persistent changes, however, survive reboots and require the distribution’s configuration mechanism. On Debian and Ubuntu that mechanism is netplan, which uses YAML files placed in /etc/netplan. On Red Hat systems and derivatives, NetworkManager is the common approach and is often managed with nmcli to modify named connections. For example, after testing an address with ip, you would create or edit a netplan file containing addresses, gateway4, and nameservers, then apply it with sudo netplan apply. For NetworkManager you would run sudo nmcli con mod ipv4. method manual ipv4. addresses ipv4. gateway ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4" followed by sudo nmcli con up. A common mistake is to perform testing only with ip and then assume the system will keep that state after a reboot; always commit verified settings to the persistent configuration mechanism appropriate for your distribution.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Temporary vs Persistent
Temporary (ip)
Commands change kernel state only. Use them to validate an address or route before modifying config files.
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3
sudo ip link set enp0s3 up
Ephemeral: lost after reboot.
Persistent (netplan / nmcli)
Write configuration to the distro-specific manager so settings survive restarts.
Examples for netplan and nmcli are shown on the next screens.
Checklist before persisting
  • Confirm interface name and that the temporary ip test behaves as expected.
  • Verify gateway and DNS by pinging the gateway and resolving a name.
  • Back up existing configuration files before editing.

screens.title: Persistent Configuration with netplan (Ubuntu/Debian)
screens.narratorSegment: On Debian-based systems such as Ubuntu, netplan centralizes network configuration via YAML files in /etc/netplan. A minimal static configuration includes version, renderer, and the ethernets section naming the interface. For instance, define the interface name you discovered earlier and set dhcp4 to no, list the addresses with prefix length, configure gateway4, and provide nameservers. Once you save the file, apply the changes with sudo netplan apply. A concrete example file shows the structure and how fields map to the settings the kernel will apply. Be mindful of YAML syntax — incorrect indentation or invalid keys will prevent netplan from applying the configuration. Always back up any existing YAML files. After applying, verify with ip addr show and ip route show to confirm the address and default route are present. If something fails, check system logs and restore the previous file. Remember: netplan translates YAML into the appropriate backend configuration and then applies it to the system; you do not edit lower-level files when using netplan unless explicitly required. Persistent Configuration with netplan (Ubuntu/Debian) means write a netplan yaml file with addresses, gateway4, and nameservers, then run sudo netplan apply and verify the system state.. In practical terms, create and apply a yaml configuration to set a static ip, gateway, and dns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Netplan saves YAML to apply on boot
keyIdea.text: Write a netplan YAML file with addresses, gateway4, and nameservers, then run sudo netplan apply and verify the system state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Netplan: Persistent config
Example netplan file
# /etc/netplan/01-netcfg.yaml
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    enp0s3:
      dhcp4: no
      addresses: [192.168.1.100/24]
      gateway4: 192.168.1.1
      nameservers:
        addresses: [8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4]
Replace enp0s3 with your interface name and adjust addresses to match your network.
Apply and verify
After editing the YAML, run sudo netplan apply. Verify with:
ip addr show enp0s3
ip route show
If apply fails, inspect the YAML for indentation or key errors, then restore the previous file if needed.
YAML pitfalls
  • Incorrect indentation will break parsing; use two spaces per indent level.
  • Using an incorrect interface name will silently apply nothing to the expected device.
  • Always keep a backup copy of the original file before editing.

screens.title: Persistent Configuration with NetworkManager (nmcli)
screens.narratorSegment: Red Hat and many of its derivatives commonly use NetworkManager to manage connections. The recommended command-line tool is nmcli. Start by identifying the connection name with nmcli con show. Then modify the connection to set ipv4. method manual and provide ipv4. addresses, ipv4. gateway, and ipv4. dns. For example, you would run sudo nmcli con mod "Wired connection 1" ipv4. method manual ipv4. addresses 192.168.1.101/24 ipv4. gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4" and ensure the interface is bound with sudo nmcli con mod "Wired connection 1" connection. interface-name enp0s3. After modifying, activate the connection with sudo nmcli con up "Wired connection 1". Verify with ip addr show and ip route show to confirm the address and default route. A frequent mistake is forgetting to bind the connection to the correct interface name, which leaves settings applied to a different device or no device at all. Always list connections and the system’s interface names first so you update the intended record. After confirming, these changes persist across reboots because NetworkManager stores them in its connection database. Persistent Configuration with NetworkManager (nmcli) means identify the connection, set ipv4.method to manual, provide address/gateway/dns, bind to the interface, then bring the connection up.. In practical terms, modify a named connection on red hat-based systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Identify the connection, set ipv4.method to manual, provide address/gateway/dns, bind to the interface, then bring the connection up.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › NetworkManager: nmcli
Identify and modify a connection
nmcli con show
sudo nmcli con mod "Wired connection 1" ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.101/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4"
sudo nmcli con mod "Wired connection 1" connection.interface-name enp0s3
sudo nmcli con up "Wired connection 1"
Replace the connection name and interface name to match your system.
Verification
After bringing the connection up, check the assigned address and routing with ip addr show and ip route show. If the settings don’t appear, confirm the connection name and interface binding.
ip addr show enp0s3
ip route show
Common pitfall
Not binding the connection to the correct interface leaves the configuration unassigned. Always confirm interface names using ip addr show before changing a connection.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Workflow: ping, traceroute, dig
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting is fastest when you follow a sequence that narrows the fault domain. Start locally: run ip addr show and ip route show to confirm the interface has an IP and a default route. Next, ping your default gateway; failure here usually indicates a local link or address problem. If the gateway responds, ping an external IP such as 8.8.8.8 — a successful ping shows routing beyond your LAN is working. If you can reach an external IP but not a hostname, the issue is likely DNS; use dig or nslookup to query your configured DNS servers directly and inspect the answer section. When packets fail between you and the destination, traceroute or tracepath reveals where the path halts, helping you identify a misbehaving hop or an upstream filtering point. A concrete example: you can ping 192.168.1.1 (gateway) and 8.8.8.8 but not google. com — dig google. com @8.8.8.8 should return an A record, and a failure points to DNS configuration or DNS server reachability. A common misconception is to assume firewall blocks before verifying addressing and routing; always rule out addressing, link, and DNS before concluding that a filter is responsible.

narration.text: Troubleshooting is fastest when you follow a sequence that narrows the fault domain. Start locally: run ip addr show and ip route show to confirm the interface has an IP and a default route. Next, ping your default gateway; failure here usually indicates a local link or address problem. If the gateway responds, ping an external IP such as 8.8.8.8 — a successful ping shows routing beyond your LAN is working. If you can reach an external IP but not a hostname, the issue is likely DNS; use dig or nslookup to query your configured DNS servers directly and inspect the answer section. When packets fail between you and the destination, traceroute or tracepath reveals where the path halts, helping you identify a misbehaving hop or an upstream filtering point. A concrete example: you can ping 192.168.1.1 (gateway) and 8.8.8.8 but not google. com — dig google. com @8.8.8.8 should return an A record, and a failure points to DNS configuration or DNS server reachability. A common misconception is to assume firewall blocks before verifying addressing and routing; always rule out addressing, link, and DNS before concluding that a filter is responsible.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginner admins frequently run into a few repeating errors. First, using the wrong subnet mask is a top culprit: an incorrect prefix length can cause a host to treat another local device as remote, preventing direct communication. Second, mismatched interface names or editing the wrong connection record leads to changes that appear to have no effect. Always confirm interface names with ip addr show and connection names with nmcli con show or by listing files in /etc/netplan. Third, forgetting to apply persistent configuration is common — changes made with ip will vanish after reboot. Make it a habit to test temporarily then write the persistent configuration and apply it. Fourth, DNS misconfiguration causes confusing symptoms: the machine can reach external IPs but cannot resolve names. Use dig to test the configured nameserver explicitly. Finally, forgetting to bind the NetworkManager connection to the correct interface leaves the configuration unattached. Quick checks: validate the prefix, ping the gateway, ping an external IP, and run a DNS query. These simple steps catch most mistakes before they become incidents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. fullNarratorScript:
Networking underpins every service you run on Linux. In this lesson you will learn the essential concepts — what an IP address does, why a subnet mask separates network from host, the role of a default gateway, and how DNS converts domain names into addresses. You will also become familiar with the practical commands used day-to-day: the ip command for inspecting interfaces and routes, netplan for persistent configuration on Debian and Ubuntu systems, and NetworkManager controlled by nmcli on Red Hat variants. Finally, we walk through a troubleshooting checklist using ping, traceroute, and DNS queries so you can identify whether a problem is local, routing-related, or DNS-related. This knowledge matters because misconfigured addressing or gateways will isolate a server, while DNS problems can make working services appear broken even when the network path is sound. As you move through the screens, you’ll see concrete command examples and YAML snippets, learn a repeatable verification routine, and spot common beginner mistakes like incorrect subnet masks or forgetting to apply persistent settings. By the end you’ll be able to configure a static IP on both netplan and NetworkManager and verify connectivity with a clear troubleshooting approach.

These objectives map to practical competencies you will gain. First, you will explain core TCP/IP networking concepts: IP addresses, subnet masks, default gateways, and DNS. Understanding these terms helps you reason about where traffic should go and why packets fail to reach their destination. Second, you will use the ip command to inspect interfaces and routes and to make temporary configuration changes for testing. This skill lets you validate assumptions before making permanent edits. Third, you will configure persistent network settings using netplan on Debian/Ubuntu or NetworkManager on Red Hat variants via nmcli, which ensures settings survive reboots. Finally, you will troubleshoot common connectivity issues using ping, traceroute, and DNS query tools like dig, following a repeatable sequence to isolate local, routing, or DNS failures. Each objective is framed for hands-on practice so you can move from reading output to making informed changes safely. As you progress, aim to connect each tool to the objective it supports and practice the verification steps until they become a checklist you can use in real incidents.

This screen focuses on practice and validation. For IP addressing and subnet masks, you will calculate network and host ranges, and then verify reachability to a gateway to confirm addressing is correct. For the ip command objective, you will run ip addr show and ip route show to read interface addresses and the routing table, and you will practice adding a temporary address with ip addr add followed by ip link set up. For persistent configuration, you will edit a netplan YAML file on Ubuntu or use nmcli to modify a named connection on Red Hat systems, and then apply and bring the connection up so settings persist across reboots. For troubleshooting, you will run a structured sequence: verify local interfaces, ping the gateway, ping an external IP, then attempt a DNS lookup. Each practice step includes a verification command so you can prove the configuration works. Practicing these steps in a safe VM environment builds confidence and prevents accidental service disruption on production hosts.

Start with definitions that shape every network decision you make. An IP address is a unique numeric label that identifies a device on an IP network; think of it as a mailing address for packets. The subnet mask is a 32-bit value that partitions that address into the network and host portions — it tells your system which addresses are local and which are remote. The default gateway is the router that forwards traffic destined for other networks; if your host has no route for an address, it sends packets to the gateway. DNS translates human-friendly names into IP addresses so you can reach services by name rather than number. A simple example: your server might have address 192.168.1.100/24, mask /24 means hosts in 192.168.1. x are local, gateway 192.168.1.1 is used for outside traffic, and DNS servers like 8.8.8.8 resolve domain names. A common misconception is thinking DNS or gateway alone will fix all connectivity. If the subnet mask is wrong, a host may incorrectly consider a peer to be local or remote, causing traffic to be misrouted even though the gateway and DNS are correct. Always verify the mask, gateway, and DNS together when diagnosing connectivity issues. Reflect: if you can ping an IP but not a name, which layer is likely at fault?

The ip command is the modern, supported utility for viewing and manipulating Linux networking. To begin, run ip addr show to list interfaces, their IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and link states. You will typically see lo for loopback and a named Ethernet device such as eth0 or enp0s3. Use ip route show to inspect the system routing table; look for a default route that points to your gateway. A practical example: when you suspect a missing address, ip addr show reveals whether the interface is UP and which addresses are configured. If there's no default route, ip route show will indicate that and explain why external traffic fails. For quick temporary testing, the ip command can add an address: use sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev enp0s3 followed by sudo ip link set enp0s3 up to bring the interface online. Remember these changes are ephemeral and useful for testing before committing persistent files. A common error is reading an interface name as permanent — interface names can differ by kernel and distribution, so always confirm the current name before scripting. After you run these commands, verify with ip addr show and ip route show to confirm your test changes took effect.

A crucial operational distinction is temporary versus persistent network changes. Temporary changes made with the ip command are applied only to the running kernel state; they are ideal for experiments, immediate troubleshooting, or short-lived testing because they are safe to revert and do not modify system configuration files. Persistent changes, however, survive reboots and require the distribution’s configuration mechanism. On Debian and Ubuntu that mechanism is netplan, which uses YAML files placed in /etc/netplan. On Red Hat systems and derivatives, NetworkManager is the common approach and is often managed with nmcli to modify named connections. For example, after testing an address with ip, you would create or edit a netplan file containing addresses, gateway4, and nameservers, then apply it with sudo netplan apply. For NetworkManager you would run sudo nmcli con mod ipv4. method manual ipv4. addresses ipv4. gateway ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4" followed by sudo nmcli con up. A common mistake is to perform testing only with ip and then assume the system will keep that state after a reboot; always commit verified settings to the persistent configuration mechanism appropriate for your distribution.

On Debian-based systems such as Ubuntu, netplan centralizes network configuration via YAML files in /etc/netplan. A minimal static configuration includes version, renderer, and the ethernets section naming the interface. For instance, define the interface name you discovered earlier and set dhcp4 to no, list the addresses with prefix length, configure gateway4, and provide nameservers. Once you save the file, apply the changes with sudo netplan apply. A concrete example file shows the structure and how fields map to the settings the kernel will apply. Be mindful of YAML syntax — incorrect indentation or invalid keys will prevent netplan from applying the configuration. Always back up any existing YAML files. After applying, verify with ip addr show and ip route show to confirm the address and default route are present. If something fails, check system logs and restore the previous file. Remember: netplan translates YAML into the appropriate backend configuration and then applies it to the system; you do not edit lower-level files when using netplan unless explicitly required. Persistent Configuration with netplan (Ubuntu/Debian) means write a netplan yaml file with addresses, gateway4, and nameservers, then run sudo netplan apply and verify the system state.. In practical terms, create and apply a yaml configuration to set a static ip, gateway, and dns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Red Hat and many of its derivatives commonly use NetworkManager to manage connections. The recommended command-line tool is nmcli. Start by identifying the connection name with nmcli con show. Then modify the connection to set ipv4. method manual and provide ipv4. addresses, ipv4. gateway, and ipv4. dns. Always list connections and the system’s interface names first so you update the intended record. After confirming, these changes persist across reboots because NetworkManager stores them in its connection database.
